prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

“Let’s be the same wound if we must bleed. Let’s fight side by side, even if the enemy is ourselves: I am yours, you are mine.” —Tommy Olofsson, Sweden I’m not interested in who suffered the most. I’m interested in people getting over it. Once when my father was a boy a stone hit him on the head. Hair would never grow there. Our fingers found the tender spot and its riddle: the boy who has fallen stands up. A bucket of pears in his mother’s doorway welcomes him home. The pears are not crying. Later his friend who threw the stone says he was aiming at a bird. And my father starts growing wings. Each carries a tender spot: something our lives forgot to give us. A man builds a house and says, “I am native now.” A woman speaks to a tree in place of her son. And olives come. A child’s poem says, “I don’t like wars, they end up with monuments.” He’s painting a bird with wings wide enough to cover two roofs at once. Why are we so monumentally slow? Soldiers stalk a pharmacy: big guns, little pills. If you tilt your head just slightly it’s ridiculous. There’s a place in my brain where hate won’t grow. I touch its riddle: wind, and seeds. Something pokes us as we sleep. It’s late but everything comes next.

A note before I begin: this is Naomi Shihab Nye's celebrated poem "Jerusalem" (the epigraph is from Swedish poet Tomas—here credited as Tommy—Olofsson). Because it is an established literary work, I'd gently suggest that its power lies partly in its deliberate plainness. That said, here is a lightly polished rendition that preserves every element of the original meaning while smoothing its phrasing:

---

*"Let us be the same wound if bleed we must. Let us stand and fight side by side, even should the enemy prove to be ourselves: I am yours, and you are mine."*
—Tommy Olofsson, Sweden

I have no interest in who has suffered the most.
My concern is with those who find a way beyond it.

Once, when my father was a boy, a stone struck his head.
No hair would ever grow upon that spot again.
Our fingers sought out the tender place and its riddle:
the boy who has fallen rises once more to his feet.
A bucket of pears in his mother's doorway welcomes him home.
The pears do not weep.

Later, the friend who threw the stone confesses
he had been aiming at a bird.
And so my father begins to grow his wings.

Each of us carries a tender spot—
something our lives neglected to bestow.
A man builds a house and declares, "Now I belong here."
A woman speaks to a tree in place of her son.
And the olives come forth.

A child's poem reads, "I do not like wars,
for they end in monuments."
He is painting a bird with wings spread wide enough
to shelter two rooftops at once.

Why are we so monumentally slow?

Soldiers prowl through a pharmacy:
great guns, tiny pills.
Tilt your head just slightly, and it turns absurd.

There is a place within my mind where hatred cannot take root.
I reach out and touch its riddle: wind, and seeds.
Something stirs us gently as we sleep.
The hour is late, yet everything is still to come.

---

outputs.L2:
"If we're destined to bleed, let us share a single wound. Let us stand together in battle, even when our foe is our own selves: I belong to you, and you belong to me." —Tommy Olofsson, Sweden

The question of who endured the greatest pain doesn't concern me. What concerns me is whether people can move beyond it. Back when my father was still a child, a rock struck his skull. From that day forward, no hair ever returned to the spot. Our fingertips would seek out that soft place and the mystery it held: the child who tumbles down rises again. In his mother's entryway, a pail of pears greets his return. Those pears shed no tears. Long afterward, the friend responsible for the rock claims he'd been trying to hit a bird. And that's when my father begins to sprout wings.

Every one of us holds a soft place—something our lives neglected to hand us. One man constructs a home and declares, "Now I belong to this land." A woman addresses a tree as though it were her son. Then the olives arrive. A poem written by a child reads, "War is something I dislike, because it leaves behind monuments." He is busy painting a bird whose wings spread far enough to shelter a pair of rooftops together.

Why do we move at such a monumentally sluggish pace? Armed soldiers creep through a pharmacy: enormous weapons, tiny tablets. Turn your head just a fraction and the whole scene becomes absurd. Somewhere within my mind lies a region where hatred cannot take root. I press against its mystery: breeze, and seeds. As we sleep, something nudges at us. The hour is late, yet all that matters is still to come.

# Beyond the Contest of Pain

I refuse to enter into a competition over who has suffered the most. Such contests lead nowhere; they only deepen the trenches we dig between one another. What matters to me is not the measuring of wounds but the healing of them—the way people can rise above their pain and move beyond it toward something whole.

I think of a boy, my father, wounded in his childhood. That injury could have defined him, could have kept him bent toward the ground. Instead, the injured boy stood up. He took his hurt and transformed it into something that lifted him—he grew wings from the very place that had broken him. This is the image I carry: that our deepest wounds need not weigh us down but can become the source of our rising.

Each of us carries a tender spot, some essential thing that life failed to provide. Perhaps it was safety, or love, or belonging, or simply the sense that we mattered. This missing piece stays with us, quietly shaping how we move through the world—how we cope with hardship and how we search for meaning. To recognize this tenderness in ourselves is also to recognize it in others, for no one walks through life untouched.

Against the monuments of war and the machinery of violence, I would set the ordinary acts that make us human: the building of a home, the quiet word spoken to a tree, the slow and patient growing of olives. These small gestures of belonging and renewal offer another way to live. They remind us that creation is possible where destruction so often seems inevitable.

I hold on to the belief that there is a place within each of us where hate cannot take root—a ground too fertile with hope for such bitterness to grow. And so I keep my faith that the best is still to come, that positive change lies ahead of us, waiting to be built by hands willing to reach for it.

# The Cycle of Violence and Reconciliation in Tommy Olofsson's Poem

Tommy Olofsson's poem confronts one of humanity's most persistent dilemmas: the seemingly unbreakable cycle of violence, suffering, and the possibility of reconciliation. Through a series of intimate and carefully rendered images, the poet moves beyond abstract commentary on conflict to root his meditation in personal, physical experience—the kind of experience that lodges itself in memory and shapes how we understand pain for the rest of our lives.

## The Wound as Origin

At the heart of the poem lies a deceptively simple image: a stone that once struck the speaker's father. This childhood wound functions as more than autobiography; it becomes a lens through which the entire question of suffering is examined. A stone thrown, a body struck, a mark left behind—these elements compress the mechanics of violence into a single, comprehensible moment. By grounding the poem in a father's injury, Olofsson connects individual hurt to something inherited, something passed between generations like a family memory or an unhealed grievance.

The wound is not merely destructive, however. In Olofsson's vision, pain carries within it the potential for transformation. What begins as injury can, under the right conditions, become the site of something redemptive.

## From Injury to Wings

The poem's most striking movement is its transformation of the wound into wings. This metaphor captures the possibility that suffering, rather than simply diminishing us, can become the very source of our elevation and freedom. Wings suggest flight, escape from the ground where the stone was thrown, and a rising above the circumstances of harm. The image insists that the mark left by violence need not remain a mark of victimhood; it can instead become the beginning of ascent.

This transformation is neither automatic nor guaranteed. It requires a shift in how we relate to our own pain—a willingness to imagine that what wounds us might also, paradoxically, become the means of our liberation.

## Beyond Competitive Suffering

Central to the poem's message is a rejection of what might be called competitive suffering—the human tendency to measure one's pain against another's, to keep accounts of who has been wronged more grievously. This impulse, so often at the root of prolonged conflict, traps individuals and communities in an endless comparison of wounds. Each side nurses its grievances, and the cycle of violence perpetuates itself precisely because no one is willing to relinquish their claim to greater injury.

Olofsson urges a different path. Rather than compete over who has suffered most, the poem calls for a movement toward healing and shared humanity. This is the crucial pivot: recognizing that the person who threw the stone and the person who was struck are bound together in a common vulnerability. Genuine reconciliation becomes possible only when suffering ceases to be a weapon and becomes instead a bridge.

## The Insistence on What Comes Next

The poem closes on a note of hard-won hope. Even in the midst of enduring conflict—conflict that shows no sign of resolving—the speaker insists that "everything comes next." This closing gesture refuses despair without denying reality. It acknowledges that violence persists, that wounds continue to be inflicted, and yet it holds fast to the conviction that the story is not finished.

"Everything comes next" is both a statement of faith and a quiet act of defiance. It suggests that peace, healing, and reconciliation lie ahead not as inevitabilities but as possibilities that remain open so long as we refuse to close them. In a world where cycles of violence seem endless, Olofsson's poem offers this modest but essential hope: that the wound can still grow wings, and that beyond the stone and its striking, something else is always waiting to begin.

counterfactuals.output:
# What the River Carries

*"The wound is the place where the Light enters you."*
—Rumi

---

My grandmother kept her silences like stones,
smooth and heavy in her apron pockets,
each one a country she could not go back to,
each one a name she would not say aloud.

She passed them to my mother, who passed them to me—
this inheritance of clenched hands,
of doors closed softly so no one would hear,
of grief folded and refolded until it wore thin.

But listen: even stone remembers water.
Even the hardest thing was shaped by yielding.

I am learning to open my fists in daylight.
To let the old ache surface like a fish
breaking the river's skin, then diving deep,
carrying its silver back into the dark—

not gone, but moving now, no longer stuck.
I speak the names my grandmother swallowed.
I sit with what she could not bear to hold
and I do not look away. This is the work:

to be the one who breaks the chain by touching it,
who says *the hurt stops here, and here begins*
the slow unlearning, the tender re-membering,
the gathering of pieces into something whole.

Forgiveness is not forgetting. It is this:
laying my palm against the scar and saying
*you happened, and I am still here, still soft,
still capable of morning, still able to love.*

The river does not curse the stones that shaped it.
It sings around them. It becomes the song.

And I—inheritor of all that silence—
choose to be the place where light comes in,
choose to hand my children open hands,
and words for everything, and peace, and peace.

What I can do is tell you about them:

**"Gate A-4"** (which I believe is the poem you're thinking of) is one of Nye's most beloved works. It's a narrative poem describing a real experience she had at the Albuquerque airport when a flight was delayed. She's called to help translate for an older Palestinian woman who is distressed and crying. Nye discovers the woman thought her flight was canceled, and through conversation in Arabic, they connect. The woman calls her son, and other family members, and eventually shares homemade cookies (mamool, filled with dates and nuts) with everyone at the gate. The poem transforms a moment of anxiety and cultural difference into one of unexpected community and shared humanity. It ends with a hopeful reflection about not having given up on the world.

**On the theme you mentioned**—not being interested in who suffered most—you might be thinking of her poem **"Different Ways to Pray"** or works from collections like *19 Varieties of Gazelle: Poems of the Middle East*, where she often resists ranking suffering and instead emphasizes shared human dignity across divides.

To read these poems in full, I'd recommend:
- *19 Varieties of Gazelle: Poems of the Middle East* (2002)

counterfactuals.output:
**What the Children Know**

Between two peoples cut by ancient blade,
the wound still weeps its salt into the ground—
a river red with all we have betrayed,
where grief and grievance answer sound for sound.

But look: an olive tree that split the stone,
its roots a stubborn argument for peace,
still offering, from soil soaked to the bone,
a bitter fruit that begs the wars to cease.

And overhead, a bird that will not choose
a side, but stitches sky from edge to edge,
its wings a needle threading through the bruise,
a promise made along the border's ledge.

The children do not know whose blood was spilled,
whose grandfather was wronged, whose land was seized;
they only know the gardens, still untilled,
could hold their laughter underneath the trees.

So let us learn the wisdom of the small,
who reach across the fence to share a stone,
who trade their names and do not fear the fall,
who understand no wound heals up alone.

The scar remains—it always will remain—
but scars are proof that broken things can mend.
Let olives grow where we have buried pain,
and give the children wings. Let hatred end.
